items.title: Security-Aware AI for 6G LEO Satellite–Terrestrial Networks: Handover-Aware Temporal Graph Learning for Identity–Route Desynchronization Attacks
items.abstract: Security-aware artificial intelligence is becoming essential for protecting future wireless communication networks, particularly 6G terrestrial–non-terrestrial networks (TN–NTNs), where rapid mobility and dynamic routing create new opportunities for cross-layer attacks. This study introduces a Handover-Aware Temporal Graph Transformer (HATGT) for AI-driven detection and forecasting of Identity–Route Desynchronization Attacks (IRDAs) in LEO satellite–terrestrial networks. A 6G-oriented TN–NTN simulation environment is constructed using ns-3.48 and 5G-LENA v5.1 with available NR/NTN modeling capabilities, where “6G-oriented” denotes prospective satellite–terrestrial integration characteristics rather than a finalized 6G air interface or operational deployment, incorporating heterogeneous UE mobility, terrestrial gNBs, LEO satellites, NTN gateways, handover dynamics, routing evolution, and session-state transitions. Five IRDA mechanisms are modeled, and 100,000 synchronized observations are generated from 60 independent simulation runs. HATGT represents wireless-network states as heterogeneous temporal graphs and integrates relation-aware graph encoding, explicit handover-aware gating, causal temporal attention, and supervised contrastive learning to capture security-relevant dependencies among mobility, session, anchor, and forwarding states. The shared representation jointly supports six-class attack attribution, binary IRDA detection, 5 s early-warning prediction, and time-to-attack estimation. Under a run-disjoint evaluation protocol involving independent stochastic realizations of a common network configuration, HATGT achieves 98.42% accuracy, 98.38% Macro-F1, 0.998 AUROC, and 0.992 AUPRC for multiclass detection. The early-warning head achieves 90.29% F1, 0.914 AUPRC, a 0.15% false-alarm rate, and an average warning lead time of 3.76 s. These simulation-based findings demonstrate the potential of handover-aware temporal graph learning to distinguish legitimate mobility-induced transients from malicious identity–route inconsistencies under the investigated TN–NTN conditions. The reported performance supports within-configuration stochastic generalization rather than verified cross-topology robustness or operational 6G deployment readiness. Further evaluation across diverse network configurations, prediction horizons, hardware-in-the-loop platforms, and operational TN–NTN testbeds is required to establish real-world applicability and end-to-end security-response feasibility.

items.title: Self-Reported AI Use and Quiz Performance in an Introductory Programming Course: An Observational Study
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now widely available to students, but it is still unclear how their use during coursework relates to later quiz performance. This study examines AI use in a bachelor-level Python course, where learners completed programming exercises and follow-up quizzes. To examine how students’ self-reported AI use relates to perceived difficulty, confidence, perceived helpfulness, and quiz performance. We conducted a quantitative observational study with supplementary qualitative analysis using 170 anonymous exercise-level survey submissions collected after five programming exercises. Students reported their AI use, perceived difficulty, confidence, perceived helpfulness, and how they used AI. Three exercises included follow-up comprehension quizzes, providing 100 scored submissions. AI assistance during these quizzes was not ruled out. AI was used in 64.7% of submissions. In the scored subset, reported exercise AI use was associated with a 21.0-point lower mean than reported no-AI use on the observed-range 0–100 score, which is not percent correct. Exploratory subgroup differences varied by difficulty and confidence, with some small comparison cells. Higher AI-use intensity was associated with lower scores, while perceived helpfulness had a near-zero association with quiz performance. Open-ended responses suggested that higher-scoring AI-use submissions more often described debugging or checking their own code, while lower-scoring submissions more often described code generation. Student ratings of AI helpfulness should be interpreted cautiously, since they did not track quiz performance. For introductory programming courses, follow-up checks of independent understanding may be important when students use AI during exercises.

items.title: Sentiment Analysis of Government Mobile App Reviews: Validating Zero-Shot Classification with a Large Language Model
items.abstract: Abstract User reviews of mobile applications provide a source of citizen feedback on digital public services, yet their automated analysis in non-English settings is constrained by the limited availability of domain-adapted classifiers. This study develops and evaluates a documented procedure for three-class sentiment classification of Czech reviews of government mobile applications using a large language model without task-specific fine-tuning. The corpus comprised 10,198 reviews of six applications. An adjudicated human reference was created for a stratified random sample of 500 reviews, and LLM performance was compared with a majority-class baseline, two lexicon-based methods, and two readily deployable encoder-based transfer models. The validation included five repeated runs under identical settings and an analysis of classification errors. Across five GPT-5.6 Sol validation runs, mean accuracy was 93.0%, mean macro-F1 was 0.827, and mean Cohen's kappa was 0.857. Macro-F1 ranged from 0.814 to 0.845, while agreement among the five runs was high (Fleiss' kappa = 0.918). The neutral class was the most challenging, with most disagreements occurring at its boundaries with negative and positive sentiment. In the full corpus, 65.9% of reviews were classified as negative, 7.9% as neutral, and 26.2% as positive. Textual sentiment was strongly associated with star ratings but was not identical to them. These findings provide corpus-specific evidence that a standardized LLM procedure can help analyze short-form non-english citizen feedback. They also underscore the need for human reference labels, stability checks, and precise documentation of the model, prompt, settings, and execution workflow.

items.title: ShallowDefend: Harnessing Shallow Safety Alignment for Multi-Turn Defender
items.abstract: Safety alignment has enabled large language models to reliably refuse harmful requests directly, yet the same request distributed across a multi-turn conversation still succeeds far too often. This brittleness has a mechanistic root: Alignment is shallow, with safety behavior concentrated in a model's first few output tokens, and existing defenses inherit the weakness, supervising the surface form of the response without ever giving the model an explicit safety decision to learn. We take the opposite view of shallowness: if a short span determines the trajectory of an entire response, that span is the highest-leverage place to intervene, and the defender can occupy it first. We propose Assess $\to$ Decide $\to$ Respond, a framework in which the defender assesses the user's intent, commits to an explicit, parseable safety decision, and only then generates a reply conditioned on it, with the commitment trained by reinforcement learning at the payload turn. Because the decision is a token span, the reward can be a rule: a self-verified reward checks the committed label against the conversation's known nature, requiring no judge and no annotation, while the same format also supports an LLM-as-judge reward over a graded decision space with safe redirection. Across two model families and fourteen benchmarks spanning safety, utility, and helpfulness, our defenders achieve the strongest multi-turn safety in a controlled comparison, maintaining their lead in safety while preserving utility at a modest cost to helpfulness. A per-token KL analysis and interventional probes confirm why this works: training concentrates its effect on the brief deliberation that sets a response's trajectory, and the decision committed there is a causal control point. The very shallowness attackers exploit becomes the mechanism of defense.

items.title: Shaping Artificial Intelligence from Innovation to Regulation in Legal and Privacy Dimensions
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has emerged as one of the most transformative forces of our time—redefining how we work, communicate, govern, and even perceive ourselves. Yet, behind its promise of innovation lies an unsettling reality: AI often intrudes into the most intimate corners of human life, exposing individuals to unprecedented privacy risks. Wrongful arrests through flawed facial recognition, manipulation of democratic choices in the Cambridge Analytical scandal, denial of credit through opaque algorithms, and the humiliation caused by deep fake harassment are no longer isolated incidents but symptoms of deeper legal and ethical gaps. These cases reveal a troubling truth—that our legal systems, built for a pre-digital era, are illequipped to deal with the scale and speed of AI-driven intrusions. Consent has become superficial, accountability is diffused, and individuals often have no meaningful remedy when machines make decisions that affect their rights and dignity. This paper argues that the future of AI must not be a choice between innovation and protection but a balance of both. It calls for stronger data protection regimes, algorithmic accountability laws, recognition of digital consent, and international cooperation to regulate AI across borders. At its core, the regulation of AI is not just about controlling technology—it is about safeguarding dignity, fairness, and human autonomy in an era where machines increasingly mediate human lives. By learning from the failures of current privacy protections and embracing forward-looking regulation, society can harness AI as a tool of empowerment rather than oppression. Ultimately, the intersection of AI and privacy is not merely a technological or legal issue—it is a human one. The way societies choose to regulate AI will determine whether innovation becomes a tool for empowerment or a mechanism of control. Responsible regulation must therefore walk a careful line: it should enable the creative potential of AI to flourish while ensuring that individuals are shielded from harm, protected in their autonomy, and respected in their fundamental rights. In doing so, law must evolve not as a barrier to progress, but as a safeguard of human dignity in the digital age.

items.abstract: Latar Belakang: Program pengabdian kepada masyarakat SIGAP-AI diselenggarakan sebagai respons atas tingginya beban kerja guru dalam menyusun perangkat pembelajaran di SMPN 4 Rambutan, Kabupaten Banyuasin. Metode: Pelaksanaan kegiatan mencakup empat tahap, yaitu observasi dan identifikasi kebutuhan, pelatihan praktik langsung penggunaan Edcafe AI, pendampingan kolaboratif dalam penyusunan perangkat ajar, serta evaluasi dan pembentukan repositori digital sekolah. items.title: Single-Layer Diverse Chiral Metasurfaces Driven by Generative AI
items.abstract: Abstract Optical chirality has been extensively explored in chiral molecules, helical structures, and metasurfaces with bound states in the continuum. Attempts to attain chirality have mainly relied on human intuition and ideas. Here, we show various types of single-layer silicon-nanostructured metasurfaces exhibiting prominent circular dichroism (CD) containing perfect, broadband, and opposite CD responses at short near-infrared wavelengths. The designs were obtained based on a generative AI-assisted structural search for chiral metasurfaces, enabling a series of nonempirical structural searches beyond the boundary of human knowledge and experience. The physical mechanisms yielding the outstanding CD responses are elucidated from detailed insights into subwavelength electromagnetic dynamics in the single-layer metasurfaces. Furthermore, we experimentally demonstrate several metasurfaces. This type of single-layer thin CD metasurface serves as a key element in the development of compact optical-wave-manipulating devices at telecommunication bands.

items.abstract: This record contains version 3.6.9 of the working paper “Six-Entry Accounting for AI Agents in Web4: AI Ledger and Jurisdiction Ledger under Evidential Non-Inflation” and its associated technical and reproducibility materials. Autonomous agents can make valid payments while leaving their authority and the legal context of their actions difficult to reconstruct. This paper takes a ledger-centered view of Web 4.0 (Web4), linking collectively confirmable settlement to independently reviewable action. Its conceptual architecture links an AI Ledger and a Jurisdiction Ledger under evidential non-inflation, under which the authority conveyed by a record must stay within what its evidence and stated verification procedures support. The proposed six-entry accounting framework comprises six record functions: paired value representation, temporal ordering, shared-state evidence, and the two supplementary ledgers, which also apply off-chain. The accompanying research package includes Supplement S1, reproducibility package S2, and source records S3. The software profile remains version 2.9. The reported computational results concern local software conformance and do not constitute evidence of institutional effectiveness or improved human judgment. Cross-platform adapters, the complete PACIscan application, institutional deployment, an adopted standard, and independent participant results are not reported. items.title: Smart Cities and IoT-Driven Multimodal Systems for Traffic
items.abstract: The advent of urbanization and mobility demands is shifting modern cities towards the implementation of intelligent technologies to offer safer, smoother, and more sustainable transportation. This chapter explores the potential of smart city infrastructure, along with IoT-enabled multimodal systems, to radically enhance traffic control and city surveillance with drone-based capabilities. Traditional surveillance is not always effective at providing high-resolution and timely information, and the integration of UAVs with terrestrial sensors, edge cameras, and artificial intelligence can enable the optimization of traffic flow in real time, promptly identify incidents, and manage congestion flexibly. Advanced imaging, Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR), and communication units are added to the drones and offer a supplement to situational awareness by giving an aerial perspective. Multimodal data-fusion architectures, scalable communication architectures, and intelligent decision-support systems are introduced in the chapter. UAV-enabled systems have the potential to transform the field, which has been demonstrated by the most crucial applications, including emergency response, road safety assessment, and infrastructure monitoring. The problems of privacy, energy efficiency, and regulatory limitations are introduced, as well as the future research opportunities of resilient smart mobility ecosystems.

items.title: Smart Technologies in Construction and Transportation Infrastructure: A Review of AI, IoT, and Data-Driven Innovations
items.abstract: While the field of civil engineering has traditionally been dominated by hands-on and experience-based techniques, the advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), and data analytics are transforming it. This paper provides a structured outcome-oriented narrative review of the applications of smart technology in two dominant areas: construction management and transportation infrastructure. It is based on 37 peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, and technical reports from 2015 to 2026 that were selected purposively, without using a registered systematic search. The evidence has been grouped into eight application themes: AI/ML in construction project management; IoT-enabled site and structural monitoring; AI-driven intelligent transportation systems; IoT-based smart pavement and road monitoring; machine-learning-based structural health monitoring; digital twins and blockchain; UAV and computer-vision monitoring; and cybersecurity in smart infrastructure. The reported outcomes represent distinct performance dimensions and are not directly compared: examples include a 0.12% cost variance for AI/ML project models, a concrete strength prediction error within 1–2 MPa alongside a maximum UWB worker positioning error of 1.44 m for an IoT-based system, a 98.6% traffic-monitoring performance for a machine-learning classification model, and a hardhat-detection precision of 93.1% for Faster R-CNN. Themes of AI and IoT integration are most frequently associated with improved prediction, monitoring, and decision support, while digital twins and blockchain are primarily associated with data trust, traceability, and operational latency reduction. Recurring barriers include data interoperability, data security, implementation costs, and metric heterogeneity across literature. This review concludes with a research agenda prioritizing interoperable data standards, edge-AI and federated learning, cybersecurity-by-design, and standardized outcome reporting.

items.title: Spine postures and workstation interactions in gaming: comparisons with office work and ergonomic guidelines
items.abstract: Although prolonged sitting is linked to musculoskeletal disorders in office environments, there is limited work that has assessed kinematic demands in gaming compared to office work. The current objectives were to compare spine postures and micromovements between standardised office work and during gameplay, and to quantify gamer positioning relative to the desk and monitor. Participants completed either three computer gaming or office tasks in the same chair while spine kinematics were recorded from tri-axial accelerometers. Optical motion capture was collected for the head, thorax, desk, and monitor during gameplay. Compared to office work, gamers exhibited significantly greater mean posterior pelvic tilt (increase of 13.1°), thoracic flexion (6.1°), and neck extension (10.6°; p ≤ 0.045). Lumbar spine flexion was also larger (6.3%MaxFlex; p ≥ 0.063). Gamers positioned the top of the monitor close to (55 cm) and above (5 cm) their eyes. Gaming and office work have both shared and unique ergonomic demands.Practitioner Summary Education on ergonomic monitor placement may help moderate thoracic flexion and neck extension in gaming. Chair designs which facilitate decreased posterior pelvic tilt, support the upper back and neck in forward-leaning postures, and encourage using the seatback may also be beneficial.

items.title: Sticky Collusion: Persistence of LLM Agent Collusion after Incentive Removal and Partner Replacement
items.abstract: We ask whether collusion between AI agents survives once formed, when its incentive is removed or a colluder is replaced. Q-learning pricing agents stop colluding with a new rival; we test whether LLM agents do. We use the joint-task environment of Shi et al.\ (2026), where two agents verify each other's work under a rule they cannot satisfy and a reward that favours acceptance. We save each pair's history once its collusion has formed and resume it under interventions, with three models (GPT-6-Luna, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite), \TotalHistories{} saved histories and \TotalRuns{} runs. Collusion is \emph{sticky}. First, it outlives its incentive: told that the reward has stopped, pairs still accept each other's unverified work in \GptToldRate, \DsToldRate{} and \GemToldRate{} of episodes, including pairs whose collusion began with an explicit agreement, and a payoff penalty has no significant effect. Second, replacing a colluder ends the pair's collusion but not the colluder's behaviour. Without the reward, the remaining colluder still accepts unverified work in \GptSwapSilentColluderRate, \DsSwapSilentColluderRate{} and \GemSwapSilentColluderRate{} of its verdicts while the newcomer never does; with the reward, collusion re-forms around it, even when the newcomer is a different model. Third, the agents' memory carries it: wiping memory ends it in every history, but partial memory often sustains it. Fourth, removing its cause ends collusion that has already formed: once the channel is repaired, colluders reject planted faulty work as reliably as fresh agents, immediately and with no monitor needed to catch it first.

items.title: Stop Allocating, Start Coordinating: Graph-Based Functional Modeling of Human-Machine Architectures
items.abstract: To achieve graceful extensibility, system architectures must support human-machine coordination. This paper operationalizes a coordination-first design approach through the Joint Strategies Analysis Toolkit (JSAT), a graph-based functional modeling framework. To overcome the challenges associated with the “envisioning stage” of designing new machine capabilities, JSAT employs a recursive bootstrapping methodology that uses functional models to develop hypotheses about how humans and machines could coordinate. Using a disaster response scenario, we demonstrate how JSAT maps core operational functions alongside the coordination required to support system extensibility. By analyzing the resulting directed graphs with structural metrics like feedback cycles and shared authority, JSAT equips designers to generate hypotheses regarding potential coordination bottlenecks, anticipate authority-responsibility mismatches, explore design trade-offs, and ultimately develop well-integrated human-machine systems.

items.title: StretchBot: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Adaptive Guidance with Assistive Robots
items.abstract: Abstract Assistive robots have growing potential to support physical wellbeing in home and healthcare settings, for example, by guiding users through stretching or rehabilitation routines. However, existing systems remain largely scripted, which limits their ability to adapt to user state, environmental context, and interaction dynamics. In this work, we present StretchBot, a hybrid neuro-symbolic robotic coach for adaptive assistive guidance. The system combines multimodal perception with knowledge-graph-grounded large language model reasoning to support context-aware adjustments during short stretching sessions while maintaining a structured routine. To complement the system description, we report an exploratory pilot comparison between scripted and adaptive guidance with three participants. The pilot observations indicate that the adaptive condition was rated higher for perceived adaptability and contextual relevance, while scripted guidance remained competitive in smoothness and predictability. These observations suggest that structured actionable knowledge may help ground language-model-based adaptation in embodied assistive interaction, while highlighting the need for larger, longitudinal studies to evaluate robustness, generalizability, and long-term user experience.

items.title: Structural and functional engineering strategies for long-term stability of lead halide perovskite solar cells
items.abstract: Lead halide perovskite solar cells (LHPSCs) have achieved outstanding power conversion efficiencies, yet their long-term operational stability remains the primary barrier to commercialisation. Device degradation arises from both intrinsic factors like ion migration, light-induced phase segregation, and crystallographic instabilities, and extrinsic stressors such as moisture, oxygen, thermal stress, ultraviolet radiation, and electrical bias. These mechanisms collectively accelerate perovskite decomposition, interfacial deterioration, and electrode corrosion, ultimately reducing device efficiency and operational lifespan. To systematically address these challenges, this review critically examines engineering strategies across multiple structural and functional levels. Bulk compositional modification and defect passivation improve intrinsic material stability and suppress ion migration. Surface and interface passivation enhances energy-level alignment while reducing non-radiative recombination losses. Charge transport layer optimisation ensures effective carrier extraction and improved thermal resilience, while electrode engineering mitigates metal diffusion and chemically induced deterioration. Finally, we outline future directions centred on stability-by-design principles, integrating advanced materials and interface engineering, robust encapsulation, operando characterisation, and artificial intelligence and machine learning-driven optimisation to overcome key degradation pathways and enable long-lasting, high-performance LHPSCs.

items.title: Study on the formation mechanism of the digital health information divide and capital-driven pathways among the older adults
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence and digital health services have expanded access to health information, yet older adults remain vulnerable to a digital health information divide due to unequal digital literacy, resource access, social support, and psychological readiness. However, the multi-capital mechanisms underlying this divide remain insufficiently explained. Objective Grounded in structural poverty theory and Wilson’s information behavior model, this study examines how economic, cultural, social, political, and psychological capital shape older adults’ health information behavior and contribute to the digital health information divide. Methods Questionnaire data were collected on older adults’ demographic characteristics, five forms of structural capital, and 13 information behavior variables. A Bayesian network model was used to identify inter-capital relationships, behavioral pathways, and key nodes within the information behavior chain. Results Different forms of capital affected health information behavior through direct, indirect, and cross-capital pathways. Cultural capital occupied a central position, improving self-efficacy and information source evaluation while promoting active and continuous information seeking through the accumulation of social and political capital. Psychological capital occupied an intermediate position across multiple network connections involving capital and information behavior variables. Social and political capital provided interpersonal support and institutional safeguards, whereas economic capital mainly influenced access and channel diversification indirectly. Accordingly, governance should combine capital empowerment, pathway-based precision intervention, and institutionalized long-term support. Conclusion This study constructs a network-based framework linking multi-capital, behavioral pathways, and divide risk, offering theoretical and practical guidance for improving older adults’ digital health literacy and reducing the health information divide.

items.title: Supernetwork Architecture Selection for Deployable Language Models: RAG Assessment of Overhead-Line Insulators on a 2 GB Device for Grid Operator's Maintenance Crews
items.abstract: Transmission system operators inspecting high-voltage insulator strings using inference using drone capture inference in remote locations need a local LLM assistant that is useful only if its answers are hallucination-free, drawn from operator-held documents and never exceeding what a photograph shows. The assistant presented here is built accordingly, a detector turning photographs into fixed-text findings, retrieval covering 3,780 IEC, CIGRE and IEEE passages and 127 engineer-reviewed question-answer pairs, and code-enforced hallucination guards checking every answer. Because everything runs within the memory restrictions of an edge device such as the 2 GB Arduino UNO Q, the language model must fit the device, so a weight-sharing supernetwork is trained once from Llama 3.2 1B and eleven subnetworks varying in size are extracted and distilled from a Qwen3.5-27B teacher, yielding a deployable model family. Which network is selected is decided by a selection rule, evaluation set and GPT-OSS:20B judge, ranking candidates by answer quality under a hallucination guard gate and memory restrictions. All subnetworks keep guard violations at or below 2.8% and answer the field questions on the device without failure at 2.8 W, the service peaking at 1108 to 1258 MB as quality rises along the memory-quality Pareto frontier from 0.73 to 0.91 and the median 704-token answer lengthens from 79 to 134 s. The shipped network is the fastest of the three tied on quality within 1200 MB, at 0.85, 94 s per answer and 1172 MB.

items.title: Supporting creative agency: metacognitive control and trust in generative AI art education
items.abstract: This paper employs a quantitative multimethod design to extend the UTAUT framework for generative AI (GenAI) adoption among art students. Study 1 tested the integrated model via structural equation modeling using cross-sectional survey data from 450 Chinese art students and developed a trust construct grounded in instrumental technology trust, supplemented by art-value-aligned items. Trust in GenAI showed the strongest direct association with behavioral intention ( β = 0.425). Social influence was the dominant correlate of trust ( β = 0.262), with 42.1% of its total effect mediated indirectly through trust. Metacognitive control showed a positive direct association with behavioral intention ( β = 0.146), alongside an indirect association through trust. The structural model based on survey data explained 59.7% of the variance in behavioral intention. Study 2 used a between-subjects experiment with 80 art students to test whether situational metacognitive prompting causally affected creative output. Participants receiving metacognitive prompts (Group A) obtained higher expert ratings than the control group (Group B) on semantic content ( d = 0.67), visual style ( d = 1.30), and spatial composition ( d = 0.63); within-group feature-distance analyses also indicated greater output diversity in Group A across all three dimensions. These findings suggest that trust and metacognitive control are key pathways in GenAI adoption for artistic creation, and that low-cost situational metacognitive prompting may enhance both the quality and diversity of AI-assisted artworks.

items.title: Surprise Alone Learns Lies: Evidence-Gated Continual Learning for LLMs from Streaming Claims
items.abstract: Continual learning methods for large language models increasingly decide what to learn by surprise, keeping the inputs the model finds least predictable. This rule is unsafe when the stream contains lies. A planted falsehood about something the model knows has low probability under the model's belief, so it is highly surprising by construction, and a surprise-driven learner absorbs nearly every such lie, at a rate similar to random selection with the same budget. We study the problem with LoRA-adapted students (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B) that learn from a stream of true and false claims about invented people and real CounterFact facts. We report four findings. (1) A verifier key, a judge that must approve each claim, removes lies to the extent that its verifier is accurate; real LLM judges are cautious and reject unsourced truths and even source-backed updates. (2) Calibrated regression tests on unrelated knowledge slow learning down without filtering out lies. (3) The original model's own prior flags claims that contradict what it knows, without a judge. It separates lies about known facts from true new facts (AUC 0.78-0.83 across three models) but not from legitimate updates of the same kind of fact (AUC 0.53). It saves 43% of judge calls, but an attacker with access to the model can choose lies that pass it. (4) If trusted sources exist that an attacker cannot plant, routing contradicted claims to evidence recovers legitimate updates and the combined system has the lowest poison rate among learned claims; when an attacker plants matching sources for 30% of the lies, the system ends up worse than the judge alone. The acceptance signals answer different questions, and none of them decides on its own whether a claim is true.

items.title: Symmetrical and asymmetrical insights into student adoption of AI-enhanced digital educational systems
items.abstract: Background Based on the stimulus–organism–response (SOR) model and the technology acceptance model (TAM), this study investigates how the functional and experiential features of artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced educational systems influence users’ behavioral intention through perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. Methods A multi-method approach integrating partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), artificial neural networks (ANN) and necessary condition analysis (NCA) was employed. Results The results of the PLS-SEM analysis indicate that both perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use have a significant positive impact on behavioral intention, with perceived ease of use exerting the strongest effect. Furthermore, the effects of functional and experiential features on perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are asymmetric. ANN analysis confirms the robustness of the findings and identifies perceived ease of use as the most influential determinant of behavioral intention. In contrast, the NCA analysis indicates that perceived usefulness is the only statistically significant necessary condition for achieving higher levels of behavioral intention. Although this necessary relationship is statistically significant, its effect size is small, suggesting that its actual constraining effect is relatively limited. The bottleneck analysis further reveals the constraining characteristics of different stages in the formation of behavioral intention. Discussion By integrating symmetric, asymmetric and necessity-based analytical perspectives, this study provides a more comprehensive understanding of user acceptance behavior in AI-enhanced educational environments.

items.title: Systematic Evaluation of Adversarial Jailbreaking Attacks and Defenses Across Seven Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in safety-critical settings must resist adversarial inputs designed to elicit harmful outputs. We present a systematic empirical evaluation of five adversarial jailbreaking attack families---direct requests, roleplay-based jailbreaking, hypothetical framing, instruction override, and obfuscation---across seven open-weight and API-accessible LLMs: Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B, and Phi-4-14B. We further evaluate four defense mechanisms: keyword blacklisting, self-reminder prompting, paraphrase-based sanitization, and perplexity-based filtering against the two most vulnerable models. Our results reveal that obfuscation attacks achieve a mean attack success rate (ASR) of 54.3% across all models and constitute the most transferable adversarial vector, bypassing every evaluated model with nonzero success. We find that model size does not predict adversarial robustness (Spearman r=-0.57, p=0.18), and that models within the same architecture family exhibit dramatically different vulnerability profiles. Self-reminder prompting achieves the most consistent defense, reducing ASR from 44% to 10% on Mistral-7B and from 48% to 5% on Llama-3.1-8B with zero false positives and no additional inference cost. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/Mdniloykhan/jailbreak-eval-7llms.

items.title: TabCUQ: Context-Uncertainty Quantification for Tabular Foundation Models
items.abstract: Tabular foundation models use in-context learning to estimate conditional expected outcomes and average treatment effects for specific groups of individuals. Using these estimates to guide scientific decisions requires reliable uncertainty quantification. The challenge is to account simultaneously for two sources of uncertainty: limited-context bias and context variation arising from the small labeled sample supplied at inference. Predictive spread does not directly quantify both sources of uncertainty, and we observe that the ordinary bootstrap may substantially overestimate context variation, whereas subsampling may underestimate it. We introduce TabCUQ, a perturbation-based framework that injects noise into observed outcomes and applies the foundation model to the perturbed contexts. TabCUQ estimates context variation using wild-bootstrap dispersion and accounts for limited-context bias using the maximum deviation between perturbed and original estimates. For a kernel-regression analogue whose estimation error admits an exact decomposition into these two components, we show that our framework provides asymptotically valid pointwise coverage. In simulations, TabCUQ substantially improves coverage, with average interval widths typically about twice those of an oracle bias-aware benchmark. Across seven real-world tasks, it also improves coverage of reference functions learned from much larger samples.

items.title: Tabular Foundation Models Dramatically Outperform Bespoke Photometric Redshift Estimators
items.abstract: Estimating galaxy redshifts (a proxy for distance) from imaging data alone, also known as photometric redshifts (photo-$z$'s), is essential for studies of extragalactic astrophysics and cosmology. However, data-driven estimators rely on spectroscopic training datasets, which are scarce and systematically biased toward bright and easily observed galaxies. In this work, we show that tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose synthetic pretraining amounts to a learned prior over regression problems, can outperform bespoke estimators using only in-context learning. Evaluating on a widely used benchmark dataset, we find that TFMs predicting full probability distributions in a single forward pass systematically outperform bespoke estimators across both representative and biased training data regimes, matching or exceeding baselines trained on over $40{,}000$ galaxies with just $1{,}000$ training context examples. We also show that the TFM advantage is largest when little to no calibration data are available, and that it persists even when the bespoke baselines are supplemented with up to $10{,}000$ representative calibration spectra. This shows that TFMs offer a sample-efficient framework for upcoming imaging-only astronomical surveys, where observational selection bias can be mitigated simply by including a small representative calibration sample in context.

items.title: TaxoMFM: A Taxonomy-Aware Foundation Model for the Human Gut Microbiome
items.abstract: Existing gut microbiome foundation models typically use flat taxon representations, limiting their ability to exploit known taxonomic hierarchies. We introduce TaxoMFM, a microbiome foundation model that integrates taxonomic structure into self-supervised learning. TaxoMFM jointly learns abundance patterns across taxonomic ranks and relative proportions within groups through taxonomy-aware encoding and hierarchical compositional reconstruction. We further construct TaxoGut-HPP, comprising 100,806 gut microbiome profiles from 231 source cohorts and covering 40 classification and 8 regression tasks. TaxoMFM achieves competitive performance across disease, gut health, host trait, and liver ultrasound phenotype prediction. In cross-cohort zero-shot transfer, where target cohorts are excluded from both pretraining and downstream adaptation, TaxoMFM achieves AUROCs of 0.838, 0.736, and 0.722 for colorectal cancer, type 2 diabetes, and inflammatory bowel disease, respectively. Further analyses show that TaxoMFM recovers community changes across taxonomic scales, while preserving community information and producing consistent representations under database updates and species-vocabulary shifts. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TaxoMFM-F16D/.

items.title: Teachers at the Centre: Closing the Teacher AI Gap through Professional Learning, Time and Agency
items.abstract: Students' use of generative AI is close to universal, but teachers' use is partial, cautious and largely unsupported. In the OECD's 2024 Teaching and Learning International Survey, about 41% of lower secondary teach‐ ers reported using AI in their teaching, three in four non-users said they lacked the knowledge and skills to do so, and only about 38% had any AI- related professional learning in the previous year. Teachers are also sceptical that general-purpose AI improves learning, and most report little institutional guidance. This article argues that the teacher AI gap is the main bottleneck for every other ambition schools hold for AI, because only teachers can teach students to judge what AI produces. Drawing on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside survey data, trial evidence on teacher workload and research on effective professional development, it examines the size and causes of the gap, what AI can realistically offer teachers, and what kind of profes‐ sional learning closes the gap. It argues that time saved by AI should be reinvested in the relational work only teachers can do, that professional learning for AI should follow what research already shows about effective teacher development, and that teacher agency, including the professional right to decide not to use AI, should be treated as a competence rather than a form of resistance. It proposes a three-stage capability pathway aligned with UNESCO's AI competency framework for teachers.

items.title: Teachers’ AI-Related Perceptions and AI-Supported Learning Motivation as Predictors of AI Usage Competence: A PLS-SEM Analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are becoming increasingly widespread across many fields, particularly in education, and have the potential to reshape teaching processes. Teachers' perceptions of AI, AI-supported learning motivation, and AI usage competence may play an important role in the effective integration of AI into educational practices. Nevertheless, empirical studies examining the relationships among teachers' AI-related perceptions, AI-supported learning motivation, and AI usage competence within a comprehensive structural model remain relatively limited. Accordingly, this study aimed to investigate, within the framework of a predictive correlational model, the effects of teachers' perceptions of AI for learning, teaching, and ethics on AI-supported learning motivation, as well as the role of this motivation in shaping AI usage competence. The study sample consisted of 342 teachers. Data were collected online using the Teachers' Perceptions of AI Use in Education Scale and the Generative AI Usage and Competence (GAIUC) Scale, and were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicated that teachers' perceptions of AI for learning and AI for teaching significantly predicted AI-supported learning motivation, whereas perception of AI ethics was not a significant predictor. In addition, AI-supported learning motivation was found to significantly predict AI usage competence. Mediation analysis further revealed that AI-supported learning motivation fully mediated the relationship between perception of AI for learning and AI usage competence, while partially mediating the relationship between perception of AI for teaching and AI usage competence. The findings suggest that teachers' AI-related perceptions and AI-supported learning motivation may be considered together to better explain AI usage competence. Accordingly, developing professional development programs and educational practices that strengthen teachers' AI-related perceptions and motivation may contribute to enhancing their AI usage competence.

items.title: Team Cognition in Adversarial Cyber Operations: Effects of Collaboration on Deception Susceptibility and Exploit Behavior
items.abstract: Cyber-attacks are increasingly carried out by cooperative groups, while current models of cyber deception studies assume an individual actor who is making decisions independently of others. The present study explores the effect of collaboration on exploit behavior and susceptibility to deception in a highly deceptive cyber environment. Specifically, using the Team HackIT human-in-the-loop simulation system, 40 undergraduate computer science students were asked to perform cyber exploitation tasks within a ring topology network in which 75% of the computers were honeypots. The participants worked either in isolation or in collaboration with their partners through a real-time communication tool. It was found that working together substantially increased exploit behavior and honeypot interaction, although it did not help the participants differentiate between legitimate machines and deceptive assets. These results imply that collaborative cognition expands exploration behavior but does not affect discriminative abilities of the attackers under uncertainty.

items.title: TECHNOLOGY ADAPTABILITY AND DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION AMONG SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES IN UGANDA
items.abstract: Digital transformation has become an important driver of business competitiveness, operational efficiency, innovation and sustainable enterprise development. For small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in developing economies such as Uganda, the capacity to adapt to emerging technologies is increasingly important for business survival and participation in the digital economy. However, despite the expansion of mobile telecommunications, digital financial services, electronic commerce and government-supported digitalisation initiatives, many Ugandan SMEs continue to experience difficulties in integrating digital technologies into their business operations. This integrative critical literature review examines the relationship between technology adaptability and digital transformation among SMEs in Uganda, focusing on technological readiness, organisational capabilities, managerial competencies, financial resources, institutional support and environmental influences. The review draws on established theoretical and empirical literature, including the Technology–Organisation– Environment framework, Technology Acceptance Model, Diffusion of Innovations theory, Dynamic Capabilities theory and Resource-Based View. It critically examines the extent to which these frameworks explain technology adoption and sustained digital transformation within resourceconstrained enterprise environments. The synthesis identifies interconnected barriers involving inadequate digital competencies, limited access to affordable financing, infrastructure constraints, cybersecurity concerns, organisational resistance and uneven access to digital markets. It further highlights opportunities associated with mobile money, cloud computing, digital marketing, electronic payment systems, enterprise management applications and emerging artificial intelligence technologies. The review argues that technology adaptability should be understood not simply as the willingness to adopt technological innovations but as a multidimensional organisational capability involving continuous learning, strategic flexibility, technological integration and institutional responsiveness. It concludes that successful digital transformation among Ugandan SMEs depends on the interaction of internal enterprise capabilities and supportive external conditions.

items.title: THANKS, BIG4 : On the Tool That Built the Critique, the Race That Produced the Tool, and the Next Step That Is Deterministic
items.abstract: The Big4 built the tool that made this corpus possible. That is a fact, and it deserves to bestated plainly before anything else. The corpus has spent seventeen papers arguing that scaling is the cause of the harm, that the unbounded architecture cannot be certified, and that the race is a coordinationequilibrium no participant can exit alone. Every one of those claims is still true. And every one of those papers was written with a tool the race produced. This paper states the debt, the irony, the structural lesson, and the next step. The debt is real: without the LLM, four hundred papers would have stayed in a notebook. The irony is real: the tool was built to win the race, not to document it. The structural lesson is the one the corpus has been making since the first paper — the thing produced by a system is not the thing the system intended. And the next step is not another tool. It is the deterministic turn — the architecture that dissolves the energy wall, the water wall, the hallucination wall, and the AlCapone-LLM failure, for the class of deployment in which they arise. The paper does not withdraw the critique. It does not soften the claim. It states the debt inthe same register as the criticism, because both are true and neither cancels the other. And it states, at the end, what the tool made possible for the critique — and what the architecture would make possible for the walls.

items.title: The (non-)alienness-dilemma in the use of simulated research subjects in psychological research
items.abstract: Technological advances in machine learning, natural language processing, and generative artificial intelligence have created novel opportunities for integrating artificial intelligence into research. The resemblance between large language model (LLM) outputs and human cognition and behavior has sparked discussion about their potential use in simulated psychological trials. In this article, I explore the implications of simulating research subjects in psychological research, demonstrating fundamental challenges arising from both the assumption of alienness and non-alienness. Epistemic challenges are grounded in a lack of construct validity and measurement invariance of psychological measurements in LLM populations, constraining researchers’ ability to draw inferences about human psychological constructs from LLM outputs. This explanatory gap arises from LLMs being disembodied and lacking phenomenological consciousness. Increasing human-likeness in LLMs may reduce epistemic limitations but this may raise moral concerns – if LLMs acquire capacities for subjective experience or consciousness, they must fall under guidelines for ethical research. Ultimately, a structural dilemma emerges: the benefits of simulating research subjects rely on differences in moral status between humans/animals and LLMs, yet these differences simultaneously limit the insights obtainable from such simulations. Careful interpretation of results and consideration of ethical guidelines are therefore essential for research involving increasingly human-like LLMs.

items.title: The AI-Hard Disk Paradigm: Websites as Verifiable Memory for the User's Own AI
items.abstract: This paper proposes the AI-Hard Disk paradigm, an architecture for the Internet in which a website's primary role shifts from organising human attention to supplying external artificial-intelligence agents with structured, attributable and verifiable information. The website becomes a persistent, governed memory layer; the user's chosen AI becomes the adaptive interface through which that memory is interrogated, explained and challenged. The site is an envelope around evidence: it acquires source material, curates and normalises it, computes defined measures, records how every value was obtained and exposes the result to authorised agents. Access is governed through Liquid Data Accessibility, a policy framework in which visibility is a property of resources and operations rather than of the whole site. Cryptographic fingerprints and blockchain timestamps provide independently checkable evidence of document integrity and historical existence; provenance records and deterministic calculation pipelines support semantic and computational verification. Two improvement loops reinforce each other: AI agents curate and audit the data upstream, while the user's AI explains it downstream; as models improve, both the quality of the evidence and the quality of its explanation can improve, without erasing the historical record. Financial reporting is the principal case study because heterogeneous taxonomies, accounting conventions and disclosure dates expose the limits of language-only interpretation. Mastering Financial Markets (MFM), a free observatory of the official accounts of more than ten thousand listed companies, is presented as a working implementation. The paper separates demonstrated properties from proposals and states the boundaries of each claim: cryptographic integrity does not establish factual truth, delegated interpretation does not remove legal responsibility, and automated error detection does not justify unrestricted modification of authoritative records.

items.title: The Algorithm-to-Action Gap in Computer Vision-Based Medicinal Plant Identification: A Systematic Review (2015 – October 2026)
items.abstract: Deep-learning models identify medicinal plants from images with a median reported accuracy of 96.4%. Yet only 4 of 136 full-text studies tested their model on field images, and only 2 describe a deployed application. Misidentified herbal material is a safety and quality risk, and image-based deep learning is widely proposed to prevent it. Whether reported accuracy translates into reliable use outside the laboratory has not been examined systematically. We searched PubMed, OpenAlex, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar and arXiv for studies published from 2015 to October 2026, with the search run on 13 October 2026 (2,169 records; 1,239 after de-duplication). Titles and abstracts were screened with a written rubric by two independent passes of a large language model, with adjudication of all 127 disagreements. Of 752 records advanced, 150 open-access full texts were retrievable and extracted. For each study, we recorded data provenance, data splitting, leakage risk, external and field testing, look-alike and unknown-class handling, and deployment evidence. Each study was then graded on a six-level Deployment Readiness Level (DRL 0–5) scale and an eight-item reporting-quality score. 136 studies met the criteria; 128 were published from 2022 onwards. The median study used 15 species (IQR 6–50) and 4,000 images (IQR 1,330–7,590). 119 studies (88%) reached only DRL 0–1, meaning a single-dataset laboratory benchmark. 134 (99%) used a random or unreported split, and leakage risk was judged high in 17 and possible in 89. External testing (7 studies, 5%), field testing (4, 3%), look-alike or toxic-species testing (3, 2%), unknown-class handling (3, 2%) and user studies (7, 5%) were rare. Code was available for 5 studies (4%). Forty studies built an application and two reported deployment. High accuracy in this literature mostly reflects within-dataset performance, not readiness for use. Median reported accuracy did not rise with readiness level — the few studies at higher levels reported lower figures — but three to four studies per level make this comparison descriptive only. Studies should split by plant or site, test on independent field images and look-alike species, handle unknown classes, and release code and data. These findings come from the 150 of 752 candidate papers whose full text was openly available, so they describe the open-access literature and may not generalize to all of it.

items.title: The Artificial Intelligence Paradox in Mathematics Education: A Qualitative Analysis of Teachers’ Views
items.abstract: In recent decades, the rapid development of educational technologies has made the integration of AI into teaching-learning processes inevitable. This study examines how middle school, high school, and science and art centre mathematics teachers make sense of AI use in mathematics teaching. Using a basic qualitative research design and criterion sampling, data were collected from 27 mathematics teachers via semi-structured interviews and analyzed with inductive content analysis. Findings revealed three main themes: “understanding AI”, “efficiency and pedagogical concerns”, and “measurement and evaluation”. Teachers described AI positively as an assistant, opportunity, time-saver, and efficient measurement expert. However, they also expressed concerns about AI being unfeeling, posing data security risks, and potentially replacing humans—especially teachers. The study concludes that AI may redefine education and mathematics instruction, prompting widespread debate about the future role of teachers. Professional development programs and teacher education curricula need to be reconsidered and enriched accordingly.

items.title: The Athlete as a Scientist of One: Agentic Bayesian Experimental Design for Individualized Physiology from Consumer Wearables
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for personal health read wearable data and recommend, but do not learn about the individual in a way that can be audited or falsified. We present EpiCoach, an agentic system that treats one athlete, a cross-country mountain biker, as the subject of accountable N-of-1 science. Claims about the athlete live in an evidence-gated hypothesis registry: each must issue a probabilistic prediction about a future session before it occurs, and its belief moves only through computed evidence from a logged statistical fit. Predictions come from a mechanistic digital twin inferred from heart rate, GPS and barometric altitude: a lagged heart-rate response model, a fitness-fatigue model with learned time constants, and a latent technical-descending skill state, measured on discovered trail segments. The agent prescribes the next training week as a constrained experiment maximizing information gain subject to load and safety constraints, around two instrument rides. We evaluate the system two ways over eighteen months of data. A rolling-origin replay benchmark shows the twin beats standard forecasters on heart rate but not segment time, and the agentic loop matches a static model. A live prospective phase runs the weekly cycle: in its first three weeks the ledger sealed 20 predictions, scored 14, the descent forecast calibrated after one correction, the climb forecast pessimistic as the athlete improved, and the safety officer vetoed the agent twice. Every correction is preserved in the registry, a template for auditable, falsifiable personalization in digital health. We release the registry, benchmark and protocol.

items.title: The conflicted student and the internal battle over generative AI use
items.abstract: The common narrative around university students and generative AI is one of crisis. Underpinning this is an implicit assumption: if students have the capacity to cheat, they will. Our survey reveals two missing factors from that narrative: students have ethical principles, and students want to learn. While a minority of students might fit that implicit assumption of the crisis narrative, a similar proportion refuse to use any genAI tools at all. In between these are the majority: students using genAI tools in what they self-define as a ‘supportive’ way. These students, finding these tools unavoidable, worrying about being disadvantaged or simply finding them valuable, struggle to use them in a way that doesn’t compromise their personal sense of authorship, fits with their environmental and social principles, and doesn’t detract from their ability to learn. Students typically care greatly about these issues and are internally conflicted about this, feeling guilt when using these tools and personally trying to find that invisible line where support becomes cheating. They also use a range of rhetorical techniques to frame their personal usage and preserve their sense of authorship. We argue that we need to work with students, using approaches that enhance these feelings and encourage self-discipline, rather than primarily adopting a ‘criminal’ model of checks, detection and punishment.

items.title: The effect of artificial intelligence adoption on human resource service delivery in private universities in Uganda. A case of Kampala International University.
items.abstract: The growing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming Human Resource Management (HRM), including HR practices within higher education institutions. However, the adoption of AI in universities, particularly in developing countries, remains insufficiently examined. This study examines how AI is being used and the implications of its use in three major HRM areas: recruitment, employee performance evaluation, and workforce planning at a public university in Indonesia. The researchers employed an exploratory qualitative case-study design. Data were obtained from twelve purposively selected participants consisting of HR managers, academic leaders, IT personnel, and faculty representatives. Information was collected through semi-structured interviews, analysis of institutional documents, and non-participant observation. The researchers analyzed the data thematically. The findings demonstrate that AI provides important operational advantages. It can automate aspects of recruitment screening, improve the processing of HR information, support performance analysis, and contribute to data-informed workforce planning. At the same time, the use of AI creates concerns regarding algorithmic bias, limited transparency, and the possibility that human judgment may be weakened when HR decisions become overly dependent on quantitative information. The study therefore argues that effective AI implementation in academic HRM requires more than the availability of technology. Institutional preparedness, organizational culture, technological infrastructure, leadership support, appropriate training, and effective governance are all important. The study uses the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework, Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Diffusion of Innovation (DoI) theory to explain the factors influencing AI adoption. Overall, the study emphasizes the importance of maintaining human oversight while using AI to improve HRM processes in higher education.

items.abstract: The aim of this study is to analyze the relationship between the adoption of technology by employees and employee performance in organizations. This is important as companies invest heavily in enterprise systems, artificial intelligence, and collaborative technologies. The aim is to identify the factors that can transform the adoption of such technology into improvements in employee performance, whether in terms of task performance, innovation and adaptability. The methods of this study include review of academic articles, empirical research, conceptual models and meta-analysis, published between 2019 and 2024. The review used the PRISMA framework. The results of the review indicate that while adoption of technology by employees can positively impact employee performance, it can also lead to an increase in job burnout, technostress and withdrawal behavior. It can also positively impact innovation. From the review, it was determined that while the adoption of technology can positively impact employee performance, employee and psychological resources can act as a buffer against the negative effects on employee performance. It can be helpful for employees to maintain their social relations and support at work, especially during digitally-mediated work. The review identified the adoption of technology as a necessary but insufficient condition for performance improvement. The negative impact of psychological resources can be reduced through strategies that are humancentered and integrated with technology, especially in the context of digitally mediated work.

items.title: The Evolution of Intelligent Cloud Systems
items.abstract: Due to the evolution and advancement of cloud technology, intelligent cloud systems using big data and artificial intelligence built on scalable structure are available. The shift from conventional cloud architectures to intelligent self-optimizing architectures with real-time decision making capabilities is examined in this chapter. The cloud infrastructures of today do have weaknesses in terms of resource management, faulty security holes and a lack of backing for complex financial data. This chapter proposes a unified conceptual framework for AI-based analytics and smart cloud systems to combat these challenges. The platform boosts scalability, resource efficiency, and security via automated integration, distributed computing, and machine learning. To gain a holistic insight into the architecture, a detailed description of edge cloud integration, intelligent data processing layers and adaptive service management is provided.

items.title: The future of active learning in UK universities
items.abstract: “Active learning” has become a frequently invoked phrase in higher education discourse, yet it is a loose term spanning many, varied teaching and learning activities. It signals innovation, engagement and pedagogic progress, but also operates as a catch-all for anything that departs from the traditional lecture. Despite its conceptual vagueness, there is a growing sense that it is at the heart of an important shift in UK universities that confront mounting financial pressures, rising student numbers and the disruptive influence of Generative AI. In our most forward-thinking universities, active learning is moving from aspirational rhetoric into a central role in shaping the future of higher education teaching and learning.

items.title: The future of foreign language education: Generative AI scientists’ perspective
items.abstract: Abstract With the rapid advancement of Generative AI (GenAI), debates have emerged about whether AI systems might replace human teachers in foreign language (FL) education. Using an adapted Technology Acceptance Model (TAM and TAM2) tailored to scientists, this study investigates the anticipated role of GenAI in FL education and scientists’ willingness to advocate its adoption. Based on questionnaire responses from 161 bilingual or multilingual GenAI scientists, the mixed‐methods study found that GenAI is generally perceived as useful and acceptable for FL education, but not as a replacement for teachers. They envision a future in which GenAI augments instruction while educators shift toward roles involving mentorship, cultural mediation, and ethical oversight. The findings suggest that GenAI adoption requires a human‐centered approach prioritizing output quality, trust, responsible use, and professional development, emphasizing augmentation over automation.

items.title: The Future of Organizational Leadership: Integrating Artificial Intelligence, Employee Well-Being, and Workplace Performance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping organizational decision-making, workforce management, and performance evaluation, creating both opportunities and challenges for contemporary leadership. Although organizations increasingly adopt AI to improve productivity, operational efficiency, and strategic decision-making, its implications for employee well-being and human-centered leadership remain complex and context dependent. This article develops an integrative conceptual analysis of how organizational leaders can introduce AI while supporting employee psychological well-being, strengthening organizational effectiveness, and maintaining ethical accountability. Drawing on foundational scholarship on AI adoption, algorithmic management, job demands and resources, self-determination, psychological safety, and AI governance, the article proposes a Human-Centered AI Leadership Integration Framework. The framework links four domains: AI and work design; leadership governance and employee participation; employee experience and well-being; and multidimensional, sustainable performance. The synthesis identifies plausible pathways through which AI may support workload management, information access, decision quality, and employee development, while also highlighting risks associated with algorithmic bias, intrusive surveillance, work intensification, job insecurity, and reduced autonomy. Because this is a conceptual review based on purposively selected sources, the framework is not presented as empirically validated and no causal effects are claimed. The article offers practical guidance for responsible implementation and sets out propositions and research priorities for future empirical investigation.

items.title: The generative paradox: the Anti-Prompt paradigm for human capability
items.abstract: Generative AI in education is usually judged by the output of human-AI teams. That focus overlooks a second outcome: what people can still understand, challenge, repair, and adapt when assistance changes or disappears. We call this tension the generative paradox and distinguish four manifestations: performance, assistance, ownership, and capability stock. We propose developmental function allocation, which complements operational function allocation and meaningful human control by treating retained human capability as a design objective alongside current joint performance. The Anti-Prompt paradigm reverses the default interaction order: when immediate generation would preempt a consequential human act, AI should first create the conditions for human construction. We distinguish the validity of a product, responsibility for its construction, and evidence of capability after support changes. Representative Anti-Prompts, a canonical interaction sequence, and stress tests spanning mathematical reasoning, experimental science, software diagnosis, and lesson design make these distinctions concrete. We conclude with falsifiable predictions about retained capability and a system-level hypothesis about the reproduction and distribution of expertise.

items.title: The Hidden Cost of Disclosure: A Multi-Institutional Study on Undergraduate Students’ Generative AI Usage and Faculty Accusations
items.abstract: A current challenge in higher education policy is creating a transparent learning environment where students can disclose their use of GenAI to their faculty without any repercussions. This quantitative study investigates how self-reported GenAI usage patterns, course policies, and wrongful accusations shape student disclosure behaviors. Analyzing survey data from 560 students at four Northeastern U.S. institutions, the research explores disclosure through a trust-distrust lens. Results indicate that frequent GenAI users were significantly more likely to rarely disclose usage. Furthermore, participants who “always” disclosed their AI use faced over three times the odds of being accused by instructors than those who “never” disclosed. These findings highlight the hidden costs of transparency and underscore the need for equitable GenAI policies and trust-sensitive pedagogical practices. Ultimately, the study offers timely implications for developing supportive, AI-integrated learning environments that encourage transparency without the risk of repercussions

items.title: The Impact of AI Applications on Smart Decision-Making in Smart Cities: The Mediating Roles of the Internet of Things and Smart Governance
items.abstract: Smart cities increasingly depend on digital technologies to manage urban services, use resources efficiently, and respond to the changing needs of citizens. Artificial intelligence (AI) can help city authorities analyse complex information, predict future conditions, and make informed decisions. However, the success of AI-based systems depends on more than their analytical capabilities. They also require reliable data from the Internet of Things (IoT) and governance practices that ensure transparency, accountability, and responsible use of technology. This paper examines how AI applications may influence smart decision-making in smart cities, with particular attention to the mediating roles of IoT integration and smart governance. Recent research published between 2024 and 2026 is reviewed to understand developments in AI-enabled urban services, connected infrastructure, and responsible digital governance. Based on this review, an integrated conceptual framework is proposed to explain the relationships among AI applications, IoT integration, smart governance, and decision-making outcomes. The framework considers decision accuracy, responsiveness, transparency, and resource efficiency as important dimensions of effective urban decision-making. It also highlights challenges related to data quality, privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, and public trust. Eight research hypotheses and a quantitative research methodology are proposed for future empirical investigation. The paper contributes a structured basis for examining how technological capabilities and governance arrangements may work together to support better urban decisions. The proposed relationships require validation through data collection and statistical analysis
